metadata.purpose: Compact semantic catalog of all principle and policy sources prepared in Archon.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Enforce stringent server-side authorization checks, centralized access control logic, secure failure modes, role-based access policies, and regular re-validation of user privileges to prevent unauthorized access and privilege escalation.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Implement secure, centralized authentication mechanisms that enforce strong password management, ensure credentials are hashed and stored securely, safeguard against credential-related vulnerabilities, and utilize multi-factor authentication for high-value transactions.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Implement robust TLS for all sensitive data transmission, enforce certificate validity and integrity, prevent downgrade to insecure channels, and define character encodings while managing URL parameters to eliminate exposure of sensitive information.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Ensure cryptographic operations run on trusted server environments; master secrets are securely managed and accessed; error handling in cryptographic modules is secure; approved random generators are used; compliance with FIPS 140-2 is maintained; and key management policies follow formal lifecycle processes.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Implement strict access controls, secure data transmission, encryption at rest, and proper data deletion procedures to protect sensitive data from unauthorized access and exposure.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Employ strong typing and parameterized queries, validate and encode inputs, enforce least privilege through controlled access, and minimize attack surfaces across database interactions.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Implement robust error handling and logging practices that prevent sensitive data exposure, ensure user-friendly feedback, enforce strict access controls on logs, and maintain detailed records for security monitoring.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Implement rigorous validation, sanitization, and access controls for file uploads and inclusions, restrict execution capabilities, and ensure uploaded files are scanned for malware to mitigate attacks such as Local File Inclusion, Remote File Inclusion, and unauthorized file access.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Employ well-tested libraries and APIs, verify code integrity, minimize privilege duration, use proper synchronization, avoid direct user data execution, and rigorously assess third-party components.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Implement secure input validation, buffer size checks, proper resource management, safe string operations, and explicit memory deallocation to prevent buffer overflows, memory leaks, and code injection vulnerabilities.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Ensure safe output encoding for untrusted data across contexts like HTML, JavaScript, SQL, XML, and operating system commands to prevent injection attacks.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Implement robust session management through server-side controls, cryptographically secure identifiers, strict cookie attributes, and session invalidation to prevent fixation, hijacking, and CSRF attacks.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Maintain updated systems and configurations, enforce least privilege, secure exception handling, minimize attack surfaces, and audit security settings for robust operational integrity.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Connection strings must never be hardcoded within application source code and should instead be securely stored in an encrypted configuration file.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Use stored procedures to encapsulate data access and enable least-privilege by revoking direct permissions on base tables.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Database connections must be closed immediately after use to release resources and minimize exposure to attacks.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always replace default database administrative passwords with strong, unique credentials or implement multi-factor authentication.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Minimize database functionality to reduce attack vectors.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: All unnecessary default vendor content, including sample schemas and demo accounts, must be removed before deploying a database to any environment.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Disable or remove all default accounts from the database that are not specifically needed for legitimate operations.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Use distinct database credentials for different user roles to enforce least privilege.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Avoid directly using user-supplied input in dynamic file inclusions to prevent unauthorized access and code execution.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Require user authentication prior to any file upload operations to ensure only authorized users can submit files.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Limit uploads to only the allowed file types required for legitimate business purposes through robust server-side validation.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always validate uploaded files by checking their headers to ensure they are of the expected type, not just relying on file extensions.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Files must be stored outside the application's web context, utilizing dedicated content servers or database storage to prevent direct access.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Restrict file uploads to validated types to mitigate risks of server execution of malicious files.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Disable execution privileges in file upload directories to prevent execution of uploaded files.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Ensure secure file uploads by utilizing chrooted environments or logical drive mounting to restrict unauthorized access.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always validate file names and types against a whitelist to prevent unauthorized file access.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Avoid passing user-supplied data into dynamic redirects without strict validation.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Avoid passing arbitrary file paths; instead, use predefined index values.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Applications must never expose absolute file paths to clients.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Application files and resources must be set to read-only permissions to prevent unauthorized modifications and maintain integrity.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: All files uploaded by users must be scanned for viruses and malware before being processed, stored, or made available to other users.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always validate and sanitize untrusted input and output to prevent vulnerabilities.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always ensure that allocated buffers are sufficiently sized to prevent overflows.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always ensure that bounded string copy functions like strncpy() result in a NULL-terminated destination buffer.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always validate buffer boundaries, particularly within iterative operations, to prevent memory corruption and buffer overflows.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always truncate input strings to a safe, bounded length before passing them to string copy or concatenation functions to prevent buffer overflows.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always explicitly close resources such as file handles and connection objects rather than relying on garbage collection to release them.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Enable non-executable stack protections (NX/DEP) to prevent execution of injected code.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Avoid using known vulnerable functions that can lead to memory corruption and security vulnerabilities by replacing them with safer alternatives.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always release allocated memory to prevent memory leaks at every function exit path.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Prefer well-tested, approved managed libraries and frameworks for common tasks instead of writing custom unmanaged code that bypasses runtime safety guarantees.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Use task-specific built-in APIs for OS operations instead of issuing direct shell commands.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always verify the integrity of code and files using checksums or cryptographic hashes before execution.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always use locks or synchronization mechanisms to protect shared resources from concurrent access that could cause race conditions.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Ensure shared variables and resources are protected against inappropriate concurrent access.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Always explicitly initialize all variables and data stores at declaration or before first use to prevent unpredictable behavior and information leakage.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Minimize the duration of elevated privileges in your application.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Prevent numeric calculation errors by thoroughly understanding and accounting for your language's numeric representation limits, type conversions, overflow, underflow, precision loss, and signed/unsigned distinctions.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Never pass user-supplied data directly to dynamic execution functions.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Prevent unauthorized users from generating or modifying application code.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Thoroughly review and validate all third-party components and libraries for business necessity and security before integration.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices / GRASP graph
records.text: Ensure secure automatic updates through verification and encryption.

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Deny by default; explicitly grant the minimum required access

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Enforce access checks server-side on every request — never trust client-side gates

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use role/attribute-based access control; avoid direct object references from user input

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Log and alert on repeated authorization failures

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use vetted authentication libraries; do not implement custom auth

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Hash passwords with bcrypt, argon2id, or scrypt — never MD5, SHA-1, or unsalted hashes

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Enforce minimum password complexity; store only the hash, never the plaintext

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Implement account lockout or progressive delay after repeated failures

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use secure, random tokens for password reset; expire them after single use

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Enforce TLS 1.2+ on all connections; disable SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Validate TLS certificates; reject self-signed certs in production

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use HSTS (`Strict-Transport-Security`) with a long max-age

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Pin certificates or public keys for high-value connections

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use established, peer-reviewed libraries (libsodium, OS crypto APIs, TLS stacks)

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Never implement custom cryptographic algorithms

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use AES-256-GCM for symmetric encryption; RSA-2048+ or ECDSA P-256+ for asymmetric

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Generate keys and IVs with a CSPRNG; never reuse IVs with the same key

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Rotate and revoke cryptographic keys; store them outside the codebase

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use parameterized queries or prepared statements for all database operations — no string concatenation

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Encrypt sensitive data at rest (AES-256); use TLS 1.2+ for data in transit

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Do not store sensitive data beyond its required retention period

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Mask or truncate sensitive values in logs and API responses (e.g. show last 4 digits only)

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Apply least privilege to database credentials; separate read and write accounts where feasible

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Apply least privilege: app accounts should not have DDL or admin rights

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use parameterized queries exclusively — never build queries via string interpolation

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Disable stored procedures and features not in use

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Validate and escape all data before persistence, even from internal sources

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Never expose stack traces, internal paths, query strings, or secret values in error responses

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Return generic error messages to clients; log full detail server-side only

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Fail securely — deny access on error, never grant it

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Log authentication events, access denials, and input validation failures

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Never log passwords, tokens, session IDs, or PII

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Validate file type by inspecting content (magic bytes), not extension alone

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Reject path traversal sequences (`../`, `..%2F`, null bytes) in file paths

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Store uploaded files outside the web root; serve via a controlled endpoint

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Limit file size and allowed MIME types; scan uploads for malicious content

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Never pass user-supplied file names to OS commands or `include`/`require` calls

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Keep dependencies minimal and up to date; review changelogs for security advisories

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Remove dead code, debug endpoints, and development backdoors before shipping

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Avoid deprecated or known-insecure APIs (e.g. `eval`, `exec` with user input, `pickle` on untrusted data)

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use memory-safe languages or memory-safe APIs; bounds-check all buffer operations

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Document security-relevant decisions and non-obvious invariants inline

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Validate all input server-side; never trust client-supplied data

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use allowlists (expected values) over denylists

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Validate type, length, range, and format; reject — do not sanitize — invalid input

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Validate all data sources: URL params, headers, cookies, JSON fields, file uploads

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Reject requests with unexpected extra fields (mass assignment protection)

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Encode output for the target context: HTML entities, JSON escaping, URL encoding, shell quoting

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Never concatenate user-controlled data into HTML, SQL, shell commands, or XML

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Use context-aware encoding libraries; do not hand-roll encoding

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Generate session IDs with a CSPRNG; minimum 128 bits of entropy

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Rotate session ID on privilege change (login, role escalation)

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Set `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite=Strict` on session cookies

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Enforce absolute and idle session timeouts

records.source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference
records.text: Invalidate the session server-side on logout

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that the application only uses client-side technologies which are still supported and considered secure. Examples of technologies which do not meet this requirement include NSAPI plugins, Flash, Shockwave, ActiveX, Silverlight, NACL, or client-side Java applets.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that all application components (including load balancers, firewalls, and application servers) determine boundaries of incoming HTTP messages using the appropriate mechanism for the HTTP version to prevent HTTP request smuggling. In HTTP/1.x, if a Transfer-Encoding header field is present, the Content-Length header must be ignored per RFC2616. When using HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, if a Content-Length header field is present, the receiver must ensure that it is consistent with the length of the DATA frames.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that a user’s passwords stay valid until it is discovered to be compromised or the user rotates it. The application must not require periodic credential rotation.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that system generated initial passwords or activation codes are securely randomly generated, follow the existing password policy, and expire after a short period of time or after they are initially used. These initial secrets must not be permitted to become the long term password.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that a secure process for resetting a forgotten password is implemented, that does not bypass any enabled multi-factor authentication mechanisms.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Where shared or secret keys are used for cryptographic authentication, these should be stored using the same mechanisms as other system secrets, as documented in the 'Secret Management' section in the 'Configuration' chapter.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that the application ensures that data‑specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA).

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that key material that is used to validate self‑contained tokens is from trusted pre‑configured sources for the token issuer, preventing attackers from specifying untrusted sources and keys. For JWTs and other JWS structures, headers such as 'jku', 'x5u', and 'jwk' must be validated against an allowlist of trusted sources.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that the client only accepts values from the authorization server (such as the authorization code or ID Token) if these values result from an authorization flow that was initiated by the same user agent session and transaction. This requires that client‑generated secrets, such as the proof key for code exchange (PKCE) 'code_verifier', 'state' or OIDC 'nonce', are not guessable, are specific to the transaction, and are securely bound to both the client and the user agent session in which the transaction was started.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that, for a server‑side client (which is not executed on the end‑user device), the authorization server ensures that the 'authorization_details' parameter value is from the client backend and that the user has not tampered with it. For example, by requiring the usage of pushed authorization request (PAR) or JWT‑secured Authorization Request (JAR).

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that there is a documented policy for management of cryptographic keys and a cryptographic key lifecycle that follows a key management such as NIST SP800‑57. This should include ensuring that keys are not overshared (for example, with more than two entities for shared secrets and more than one entity for private keys).

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that all cryptographic modules fail securely, and errors are handled in a way that does not enable vulnerabilities, such as Padding Oracle attacks.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verifythattherandomnumbergenerationmechanisminuseisdesignedto worksecurely,evenunderheavydemand.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verifythatonlyapprovedcryptographicalgorithmsandmodesofoperation areusedforkeygenerationandseeding,anddigitalsignaturegeneration andverification. Keygenerationalgorithmsmustnotgenerateinsecurekeys vulnerabletoknownattacks,forexample,RSAkeyswhicharevulnerableto Fermatfactorization.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that TLS is used for all connectivity between a client and external facing, HTTP‑based services, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that an encrypted protocol such as TLS is used for all inbound and outbound connections to and from the application, including monitoring systems, management tools, remote access and SSH, middleware, databases, mainframes, partner systems, or external APIs. The server must not fall back to insecure or unencrypted protocols.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that TLS or another appropriate transport encryption mechanism used for all connectivity between internal, HTTP‑based services within the application, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that services communicating internally within a system (intra‑service communications) use strong authentication to ensure that each endpoint is verified. Strong authentication methods, such as TLS client authentication, must be employed to ensure identity, using public‑key infrastructure and mechanisms that are resistant to replay attacks. For microservice architectures, consider using a service mesh to simplify certificate management and enhance security.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that communications between backend application components that don't support the application's standard user session mechanism, including APIs, middleware, and data layers, are authenticated. Authentication must use individual service accounts, short‑term tokens, or certificate‑based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys, or shared accounts with privileged access.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verifythatanallowlistisusedtodefinetheexternalresourcesorsystems withwhichtheapplicationispermittedtocommunicate(e.g.,foroutbound requests,dataloads,orfileaccess). Thisallowlistcanbeimplementedatthe applicationlayer,webserver,firewall,oracombinationofdifferentlayers.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third‑party systems, keys and seeds for time‑based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware‑backed solution such as an HSM.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that all cryptographic operations are performed using an isolated security module (such as a vault or hardware security module) to securely manage and protect key material from exposure outside of the security module.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verifythatsecretsareconfiguredtoexpireandberotatedbasedonthe application’sdocumentation.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that communications between backend application components that don't support the application's standard user session mechanism, including APIs, middleware, and data layers, are authenticated. Authentication must use individual service accounts, short-term tokens, or certificate-based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys, or shared accounts with privileged access.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, keys and seeds for time-based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that access to secret assets adheres to the principle of least privilege.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that an inventory catalog, such as a software bill of materials (SBOM), is maintained of all third-party libraries in use, including verifying that components come from pre-defined, trusted, and continually maintained repositories.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that application documentation highlights third-party libraries which are considered to be "risky components".

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that third-party components and all of their transitive dependencies are included from the expected repository, whether internally owned or an external source, and that there is no risk of a dependency confusion attack.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that the application implements additional protections around parts of the application which are documented as containing "dangerous functionality" or using third-party libraries considered to be "risky components". This could include techniques such as sandboxing, encapsulation, containerization or network level isolation to delay and deter attackers who compromise one part of an application from pivoting elsewhere in the application.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that all proxying and middleware components transfer the user’s original IP address correctly using trusted data fields that cannot be manipulated by the end user, and the application and web server use this correct value for logging and security decisions such as rate limiting, taking into account that even the original IP address may not be reliable due to dynamic IPs, VPNs, or corporate firewalls.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that logs are securely transmitted to a logically separate system for analysis, detection, alerting, and escalation. The aim is to ensure that if the application is breached, the logs are not compromised.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that the application continues to operate securely when external resource access fails, for example, by using patterns such as circuit breakers or graceful degradation.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that the application fails gracefully and securely, including when an exception occurs, preventing fail-open conditions such as processing a transaction despite errors resulting from validation logic.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that the media server is configured to use and support approved Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) ciphersuites and a secure protection profile for the DTLS Extension for establishing keys for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (DTLS-SRTP).

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) authentication is checked at the media server to prevent Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) injection attacks from leading to either a Denial of Service condition or audio or video media insertion into media streams.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that the media server is able to continue processing incoming media traffic when encountering malformed Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) packets.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that the media server is able to continue processing incoming media traffic during a flood of Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) packets from legitimate users.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that any audio or video recording mechanisms associated with the media server are able to continue processing incoming media traffic during a flood of Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) packets from legitimate users.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Security controls should be centralized, simple (economy of design), verifiably secure, and reusable. This should avoid duplicate, missing, or ineffective controls.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Ideally, a single access control mechanism should be used to access protected data and resources. All requests should pass through this single mechanism to avoid copy and paste or insecure alternative paths.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify the use of a secure software development lifecycle that addresses security in all stages of development.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify availability of a secure coding checklist, security requirements, guideline, or policy to all developers and testers.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that an ongoing process exists to ensure that the application source code is free from backdoors, malicious code (e.g., salami attacks, logic bombs, time bombs), and undocumented or hidden features (e.g., Easter eggs, insecure debugging tools). Complying with this section is not possible without complete access to source code, including third‑party libraries, and is therefore probably only suitable for applications requiring the very highest levels of security.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that mechanisms are in place to detect and respond to configuration drift in deployed environments. This may include using immutable infrastructure, automated redeployment from a secure baseline, or drift detection tools that compare current state against approved configurations.

records.source: OWASP_ASVS
records.text: Verify that configuration hardening is performed on all third‑party products, libraries, frameworks, and services as per their individual recommendations.

records.source: CWE_Top25
records.text: Run the code in a jail or similar sandbox environment that enforces strict boundaries between the process and the operating system.

records.source: CWE_Top25
records.text: Use quotas or other resource-limiting settings provided by the operating system or environment.

records.source: CWE_Top25
records.text: Use the access control capabilities of your operating system and server environment and define your access control lists accordingly. Use a default deny policy when defining these ACLs.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text: Limit access to sensitive data based on the principle of least privilege. Only grant access to data that is necessary for the specific user or process.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text: Limit model access to external data sources, and ensure runtime data orchestration is securely managed to avoid unintended data leakage.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text: Provide guidance on avoiding the input of sensitive information. Offer training on best practices for interacting with LLMs securely.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text: Follow guidelines like "OWASP API8:2023 Security Misconfiguration" to prevent leaking sensitive information through error messages or configuration details.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text: Use homomorphic encryption to enable secure data analysis and privacy-preserving machine learning. This ensures data remains confidential while being processed by the model.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text: Maintain an up-to-date inventory of components using a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) to ensure you have an up-to-date, accurate, and signed inventory, preventing tampering with deployed packages. SBOMs can be used to detect and alert for new, zero-date vulnerabilities quickly. AI BOMs and ML SBOMs are an emerging area and you should evaluate options starting with OWASP CycloneDX

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text: Only use models from verifiable sources and use third-party model integrity checks with signing and file hashes to compensate for the lack of strong model provenance. Similarly, use code signing for externally supplied code.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text:
Avoid open-ended extensions
Avoid the use of open-ended extensions where possible (e.g., run a shell command, fetch a URL, etc.) and use extensions with more granular functionality. For example, an LLM-based app may need to write some output to a file. If this were implemented using an extension to run a shell function then the scope for undesirable actions is very large (any other shell command could be executed). A more secure alternative would be to build a specific file-writing exOtWenAsSiPo nTo tph a10t ofonrl yLL iMm Applepmliceanttios ntsh avt2 .s0pecific functionality.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text:
Sanitise LLM inputs and outputs
Follow secure coding best practice, such as applying OWASP’s recommendations in ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard), with a particularly strong focus on input sanitisation. Use Static Application Security Testing (SAST) and Dynamic and Interactive application testing (DAST, IAST) in development pipelines.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text:
Ensure that security controls are enforced independently from the LLM
Critical controls such as privilege separation, authorization bounds checks, and similar must not be delegated to the LLM, either through the system prompt or otherwise. These controls need to occur in a deterministic, auditable manner, and LLMs are not (currently) conducive to this. In cases where an agent is performing tasks, if those tasks require different levels of access, then multiple agents should be used, each configured with the least privileges needed to perform the desired tasks.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text:
Secure Coding Practices
Establish secure coding practices to prevent the integration of vulnerabilities due to incorrect code suggestions.

records.source: OWASP_LLM_Top10
records.text:
Access Controls
Implement strong access controls, including role-based access control (RBAC) and the principle of least privilege, to limit unauthorized access to LLM model repositories and training environments.

records.source: NIST_AI_RMF
records.text: AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may be said to be secure.

records.source: NIST_AI_RMF
records.text: Maintaining the provenance of training data and supporting attribution of the AI system’s decisions to subsets of training data can assist with both transparency and accountability.

records.text: MANAGE 4.2: Measurable activities for continual improvements are integrated into AI system updates and include regular engagement with interested parties, including relevant AI actors.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: Organizations should integrate the SSDF throughout their existing software development practices, express their secure software development requirements to third-party suppliers using SSDF conventions, and acquire software that meets the practices described in the SSDF.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: Organizations should ensure that their people, processes, and technology are prepared to perform secure software development.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: Organizations should produce well-secured software with minimal security vulnerabilities in its releases.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PO.2.2: Provide role-based training for all personnel with responsibilities that contribute to secure development. Periodically review personnel proficiency and role-based training, and update the training as needed.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PO.2.3: Obtain upper management or authorizing official commitment to secure development, and convey that commitment to all with development-related roles and responsibilities.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PO.3.3: Configure tools to generate artifacts of their support of secure software development practices as defined by the organization.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PO.5.2: Secure and harden development endpoints (i.e., endpoints for software designers, developers, testers, builders, etc.) to perform development-related tasks using a risk-based approach.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PS.3.1: Securely archive the necessary files and supporting data (e.g., integrity verification information, provenance data) to be retained for each software release.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PS.3.2: Collect, safeguard, maintain, and share provenance data for all components of each software release (e.g., in a software bill of materials [SBOM]).

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PW.4.1: Acquire and maintain well-secured software components (e.g., software libraries, modules, middleware, frameworks) from commercial, open-source, and other third-party developers for use by the organizations software.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PW.4.2: Create and maintain well-secured software components in-house following SDLC processes to meet common internal software development needs that cannot be better met by third-party software components.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PW.5.1: Follow all secure coding practices that are appropriate to the development languages and environment to meet the organizations requirements.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PW.7.2: Perform the code review and/or code analysis based on the organizations secure coding standards, and record and triage all discovered issues and recommended remediations in the development teams workflow or issue tracking system.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PW.9.1: Define a secure baseline by determining how to configure each setting that has an effect on security or a security-related setting so that the default settings are secure and do not weaken the security functions provided by the platform, network infrastructure, or services.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: PW.9.2: Implement the default settings (or groups of default settings, if applicable), and document each setting for software administrators.

records.source: NIST_SP800218
records.text: RV.1.1: Gather information from software acquirers, users, and public sources on potential vulnerabilities in the software and third-party components that the software uses, and investigate all credible reports.

records.text: RV.3.2: Analyze the root causes over time to identify patterns, such as a particular secure coding practice not being followed consistently.
